He relives each stage of human life in faithful obedience
He overcomes temptation where Adam and Israel failed
Obedient to death on the tree, he reverses Adam's disobedience at the tree
Risen, he becomes the head of a renewed humanity
United to him by the Spirit, believers grow toward incorruption and communion with God

positions.name: Ransom theory
positions.summary:
The ransom theory takes literally Jesus' saying that the Son of Man came to give his life 'as a ransom for many' (Mark 10:45). Through sin humanity sold itself into captivity to the devil, who thereby gained a kind of claim over sinners. God, acting justly even toward the unjust, offered Christ as the price of release. The devil accepted the exchange, but in seizing the sinless Son of God he overreached: death could not hold one over whom it had no claim, and by grasping at him the devil lost his hold on everyone else.

Gregory of Nyssa gave this its most famous image: Christ's divinity was hidden under the 'bait' of his human flesh, like a fishhook, so that the devil swallowed the bait and was caught by the hook. Augustine and others used the image of a mousetrap. Proponents stress that God did not owe the devil anything in strict justice; rather, God chose to defeat evil by fair means rather than sheer force, and the 'deception' was the devil's own blindness to divine humility. The ransom theory dominated popular piety for roughly a thousand years and lives on in Christus Victor.

figures.name: Origen of Alexandria
figures.bio: The most prolific scholar of the early church. Commenting on Matt 20:28, he asked to whom the ransom was paid; it could not be God, so it must have been the evil one who held us captive until the soul of Jesus was given, though the devil was deceived in thinking he could keep it.

works.author: Origen
works.title: Commentary on Matthew

figures.name: Gregory of Nyssa
figures.bio: Younger brother of Basil the Great. His Catechetical Oration explains salvation to catechists; it argues that God, being just, offered the devil a ransom he would accept, and that the deity was hidden under flesh like a hook beneath bait.

works.author: Gregory of Nyssa
works.title: Catechetical Oration (Great Catechism)

figures.name: Rufinus of Aquileia
figures.bio: Translator of Origen into Latin. His commentary on the creed repeats the fishhook image, carrying the ransom-to-the-devil idea into the Latin West.

works.author: Rufinus
works.title: Commentary on the Apostles' Creed

figures.name: Augustine of Hippo
figures.bio: Augustine taught that the devil was justly overcome by the justice of Christ rather than by power, and used the image of the cross as a mousetrap baited with Christ's blood. He combined this with sacrificial and mediator language.

works.author: Augustine
works.title: On the Trinity

works.author: Augustine
works.title: Sermons

figures.name: Gregory the Great
figures.bio: In his vast commentary on Job he read Leviathan (Job 41:1) as the devil caught on the hook of Christ's incarnation, transmitting the image to medieval preaching.

works.author: Gregory the Great
works.title: Moralia in Job

positions.context:
Ransom and redemption language (lytron, apolytrōsis, agorazō) comes from the slave market and from Israel's exodus, when God 'redeemed' his people from Egypt. Early Christians asked a natural question: if a ransom was paid, to whom? Origen answered: to the one who held us captive. Some Fathers rejected any payment to the devil. Gregory of Nazianzus, in his Second Oration on Easter (Oration 45), argued it could be paid neither to the robber nor strictly to the Father, and that the language should not be pressed.

Anselm's Cur Deus Homo (1098) argued that the devil had no rights at all, and the theory declined in academic theology. Yet its narrative of a deceived and defeated enemy survived in liturgy, art and literature, and the modern Christus Victor model reframes it without the devil's 'rights'. C. S. Lewis's The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe (1950), where Aslan dies under the 'Deep Magic' in place of Edmund and rises by a 'deeper magic', is a widely known modern echo. Most patristic writers combined ransom with sacrifice, recapitulation and healing.
claims: Through sin humanity came under the power of the devil and death.
Christ's life was given as a ransom to secure humanity's release.
God defeats evil by justice and humility, not mere force.
The devil, unable to perceive the hidden divinity, overreached in seizing the sinless Christ.
Death could not hold Christ, and in losing him the devil lost his claim over those who belong to Christ.
Redemption means real liberation from bondage, echoing the exodus.

scriptures.reading: The Son of Man gives his life as a ransom (lytron) for many: the theory's foundational text.
Christ gave himself as a ransom (antilytron) for all.
Ransomed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ.
The rulers of this age did not understand God's hidden wisdom; had they understood, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory, the basis for the idea of the deceived enemy.
Through death Christ destroys the one who has the power of death and frees those enslaved.
Now the ruler of this world is cast out.
Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook? Read by Gregory the Great as the devil caught by Christ.
Delivered from the domain of darkness and transferred to the kingdom of the Son, in whom we have redemption.

arguments.text: The language of ransom and redemption is pervasive in the New Testament and naturally implies a captor from whom captives are released.
Scripture presents the devil as having real (if usurped) power over the world and death, which Christ's death breaks.
Paul says the rulers of this age would not have crucified the Lord of glory had they understood God's hidden wisdom, implying a kind of divine outwitting.
God's justice extends even to his enemies; defeating the devil by fair exchange rather than force displays God's righteousness and humility.
The theory was widely held by Greek and Latin Fathers for centuries and shaped Easter liturgy, such as the harrowing of hell.
It gives a dramatic, intelligible narrative that ordinary believers can grasp, explaining salvation as liberation.

critiques.text: Focusing on a transaction with the devil narrows salvation to one moment; Irenaeus placed liberation within Christ's whole life of obedience.
Aulén kept the drama but dropped the commercial details: the ransom is a metaphor for costly liberation, not a price literally paid to Satan.
Anselm argued that the devil, as a rebel creature, has no rights that God must buy off; God owes nothing to a thief.
Abelard rejected the idea that the devil had any legitimate power, and found the transaction unworthy of a God of love.
The true problem is our guilt before God's law; the devil's power is that of an accuser, which falls once the penalty is paid to divine justice.
It makes the devil, rather than God's moral government, the party whose claims must be satisfied, reversing the moral order.
Girard valued the patristic intuition that Satan was outwitted, but held that 'Satan' names the mechanism of collective violence, not a creditor.
Gregory of Nazianzus warned that it is outrageous to suppose the robber received the price; the image should not be pressed beyond its point.

responses.text: Ransom is the climax of a whole life given (Mark 10:45 speaks of a life of service ending in death) and fits within recapitulation, as Irenaeus himself shows.
Defenders grant that the details are imagery, but insist the core is not merely metaphorical: there is a real enemy, and he was really defeated through Christ's death.
Most ransom theologians did not grant the devil strict rights; Augustine stressed that God overcame him by justice to show that God works righteously even toward the unjust.
Ransom imagery is itself a picture of love: God pays dearly for his people. It is not cold commerce but costly rescue.
Accusation is one aspect, but Scripture also speaks of bondage, fear of death and the domain of darkness; the ransom addresses enslavement, not just a legal charge.
God's government is precisely what is vindicated when the usurper is overcome justly and his captives restored to their rightful King.
Patristic theology can welcome Girard's insight that the devil works through crowds and accusation while still affirming a personal adversary.
Nazianzen's caution is accepted by many: the theory is best held as a narrative pointing to the truth that God's humility outwits evil, not as a literal payment contract.

strawMen.strawMan: The ransom theory teaches that God owed the devil something.
strawMen.correction: Most proponents denied that God owed the devil anything; the point is that God chose to act justly rather than by brute force.

strawMen.strawMan: It portrays God as a trickster who lies.
strawMen.correction: The 'deception' is the devil's self-deception: pride cannot recognize divine humility (1 Cor 2:8). God hides his glory in weakness; he does not tell falsehoods.

strawMen.strawMan: It is a fringe idea of a few eccentric writers.
strawMen.correction: It was mainstream for roughly nine centuries in East and West and shaped liturgy and art.

positive: Takes seriously the reality of evil and spiritual bondage.
Gave early Christians a vivid, preachable story of liberation.
Highlights God's humility and the hiddenness of divine power in weakness.
Inspired liturgy, iconography and literature, including the harrowing of hell.
negative: Can suggest the devil has rights or that God engages in trickery.
Speculative details about the transaction go beyond Scripture.
Gives little account of personal guilt or moral transformation.
Its decline left many Western Christians with no theology of the powers.

adherents: Much of patristic East and West (c. 3rd-11th centuries), usually alongside other models
Popular medieval preaching and drama
Echoed today within Christus Victor proponents and in Orthodox Paschal hymnody
Popular literature (e.g. C. S. Lewis's Narnia)

proponent.author: Darby Kathleen Ray
proponent.title: Deceiving the Devil: Atonement, Abuse, and Ransom

sequence: Humanity sins and falls into bondage to the devil and death
The devil gains a hold over sinners as captives
God offers his Son as the ransom for their release
The devil seizes Christ, blind to the divinity hidden in his flesh
Death cannot hold the sinless God-man; the captor is caught
Having overreached, the devil loses his claim on humanity
The captives are set free to belong to God

positions.name: Christus Victor
positions.summary:
Christus Victor ('Christ the Victor') sees the atonement first of all as a divine conflict and triumph. Humanity is held captive by hostile powers: sin, death, the devil, and in some versions the law's curse and the wrath that falls on sin. In Christ, God himself enters the battle; through his life, death and resurrection he defeats these tyrants and liberates the world. The resurrection is not an appendix to the cross but its vindication and the public sign of victory.

Gustaf Aulén named and championed this as the 'classic' view in 1930-31, arguing that it was the dominant view of the Fathers and of Luther, and that it is 'objective' in a different way from Anselm: God is the subject of the whole work from start to finish, not humanity offering satisfaction to God. Modern proponents range from Orthodox and Lutheran theologians to Anabaptists such as J. Denny Weaver, who develop a nonviolent 'narrative Christus Victor', and evangelical Greg Boyd, who sets it within a 'warfare worldview'. Many evangelicals, including N. T. Wright, combine victory with substitution.

figures.name: Gustaf Aulén
figures.bio: Professor at Lund and later Bishop of Strängnäs. His lectures, published in English as Christus Victor, classified atonement theories into three types (classic, Latin/objective, subjective/moral) and argued that the classic victory type had been neglected in the West.

works.author: Gustaf Aulén
works.title: Christus Victor: An Historical Study of the Three Main Types of the Idea of the Atonement

figures.name: Martin Luther
figures.bio: Aulén read Luther as reviving the classic view, citing Luther's language of Christ's battle with the tyrants of sin, death, law, wrath and the devil. Others note that Luther also speaks of Christ bearing our sin and curse, so he combines victory and substitution.

works.author: Martin Luther
works.title: Lectures on Galatians

figures.name: Gregory A. Boyd
figures.bio: American evangelical pastor (Woodland Hills Church) and author who sets atonement within a 'warfare worldview' in which God battles cosmic powers; he defended Christus Victor in a multi-view volume.

works.author: Gregory A. Boyd
works.title: God at War: The Bible and Spiritual Conflict

works.author: Gregory A. Boyd
works.title: Christus Victor View
works.locator: in The Nature of the Atonement: Four Views, ed. Beilby and Eddy

figures.name: J. Denny Weaver
figures.bio: Bluffton University professor who proposed a 'narrative Christus Victor' in which God's reign confronts the powers nonviolently through Jesus' life, death and resurrection, rejecting any model in which God requires violence.

works.author: J. Denny Weaver
works.title: The Nonviolent Atonement

figures.name: Fleming Rutledge
figures.bio: Preacher whose major study of the crucifixion gives Christus Victor (with an 'apocalyptic' reading of Paul) a central place while also defending substitution, an example of combining models.

works.author: Fleming Rutledge
works.title: The Crucifixion: Understanding the Death of Jesus Christ

positions.context:
Victory imagery runs through the New Testament (the strong man bound, the ruler of this world cast out, the powers disarmed) and through the patristic and liturgical tradition, from Irenaeus to the Orthodox Paschal troparion of Christ trampling down death by death. Aulén argued that Western theology after Anselm replaced this drama with a legal transaction, and that liberal theology reduced it further to moral example.

Critics argued that Aulén oversimplified history, since most Fathers combined several images and Luther strongly affirmed substitution. Still, his book reshaped the discussion. The model was taken up in twentieth-century biblical theology (the 'apocalyptic Paul' of J. Louis Martyn and others), by Pentecostal and Global South Christians attentive to spiritual warfare, and by Anabaptists seeking a nonviolent atonement. Like other models it is commonly held in combination: many argue that substitution is the means and victory the result.
claims: Humanity's plight is captivity to hostile powers: sin, death, the devil, and the curse.
God himself, in Christ, is the active agent of salvation throughout.
Christ's death and resurrection are a decisive victory over these powers.
The resurrection is integral to atonement, the public vindication of the crucified one.
Salvation is liberation into God's kingdom and new creation.
The victory is already won but awaits final consummation when death is destroyed.

scriptures.reading: The first promise of a coming victory over the serpent.
Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them in the cross.
Through death he destroyed the one who has the power of death and freed slaves of fear.
The Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the devil.
Jesus' exorcisms show the strong man bound and his house plundered.
Now is the judgment of this world; its ruler will be cast out as Jesus is lifted up.
Death is swallowed up in victory; thanks be to God who gives us the victory.
The Lion of Judah has conquered, and he is the slain Lamb who ransomed people for God.
He ascended, leading captivity captive.

arguments.text: Jesus' ministry is framed as conflict with Satan from the temptation through the exorcisms to the cross; the atonement should be read within that story.
The New Testament's most-quoted Old Testament text, Ps 110:1, speaks of enemies made a footstool: early Christians understood Christ's work as enthronement over enemies.
Victory over death is the dominant note of early Christian worship, as in the Orthodox Paschal hymn and in early depictions of the harrowing of hell.
It keeps God as the subject of atonement from beginning to end, avoiding any split between a merciful Son and a Father who must be appeased.
It explains systemic and cosmic evil, not only individual guilt, giving the gospel social and cosmic scope.
It integrates the resurrection, which in purely legal models can seem merely a proof that payment was accepted.

critiques.text: Irenaeus's victory is won by Christ's human obedience; Aulén's emphasis on God as sole actor risks underplaying Christ's humanity, which is what makes the victory ours.
Aulén borrowed the drama of the ransom theory but discarded the mechanism that explained how Christ's death defeats the devil.
It describes a battle but not why the Son had to die; a victory by power alone does not address the moral disorder of sin before God.
Mythological language of cosmic powers can bypass human responsibility and the change of heart that salvation must produce.
It does not explain how victory is achieved; Scripture links the defeat of the accuser to the cancellation of guilt (Col 2:14-15; Rev 12:10-11), which requires substitution.
It offers no account of how God's law and justice are upheld when the guilty are freed.
Without an account of what the 'powers' are, it risks myth; Girard identifies them with the mechanism of collective violence the cross unmasks.
Orthodoxy affirms the victory but stresses that it is accomplished in Christ's assumed humanity and appropriated by participation, not only announced as a cosmic event.

responses.text: Most proponents now affirm that God conquers precisely as the obedient human Jesus; divine initiative and human obedience coincide in the incarnate Son.
The mechanism is the resurrection: the powers do their worst, and God overturns their verdict. No transaction with the devil is needed.
The Son dies because the powers act through death and must be defeated where they reign; the cross is victory through self-giving, not power alone.
The powers include human structures and choices; liberation calls for repentance and new life, and Christ's victory frees the will to respond.
Many proponents (e.g. Rutledge) agree that substitution is part of how victory is won; Christus Victor is the frame, not a denial of every other image.
God's justice is his righteous action to set the world right by defeating evil; justice is vindicated in the overthrow of the oppressor, as in the exodus.
Many find Girard's analysis a helpful account of how the powers work, while holding that the powers are also spiritual and not merely social.
Agreed: Aulén himself drew on the Greek Fathers, and victory and participation belong together in Orthodox worship.

strawMen.strawMan: Christus Victor ignores sin and only talks about demons.
strawMen.correction: Sin itself is one of the powers Christ defeats, and proponents speak of forgiveness and the cancellation of guilt as part of the victory.

strawMen.strawMan: It is a modern invention of Aulén.
strawMen.correction: Aulén named and systematized it, but its themes are prominent in the New Testament, the Fathers, the liturgy and Luther.

strawMen.strawMan: Christus Victor is incompatible with any substitution.
strawMen.correction: Some (e.g. Weaver) reject penal substitution, but many proponents combine victory with substitution.

positive: Recovers the resurrection and cosmic scope of salvation.
Speaks powerfully in contexts where spiritual oppression and systemic evil are felt realities.
Grounds Christian hope and courage in a victory already won.
Shaped liturgical renewal of Easter celebrations.
negative: Can become vague about personal guilt and forgiveness.
Aulén's historical typology has been widely criticized as oversimplified.
Can encourage a triumphalism that underplays the ongoing reality of suffering.
Popular forms may overemphasize demons at the expense of moral responsibility.

adherents: Eastern Orthodox liturgy and theology (alongside theosis)
Many Lutherans, especially Scandinavian
Anabaptist and Mennonite theologians (narrative Christus Victor)
Pentecostal and charismatic Christians emphasizing spiritual warfare
Many evangelicals who combine it with substitution (e.g. N. T. Wright, Fleming Rutledge)

proponent.author: Gregory A. Boyd
proponent.title: Christus Victor View
proponent.locator: in The Nature of the Atonement: Four Views

critic.author: Thomas R. Schreiner
critic.title: Penal Substitution View
critic.locator: in The Nature of the Atonement: Four Views

sequence: Humanity is enslaved to sin, death and the devil
God himself enters the conflict in the person of Christ
Christ confronts the powers through his ministry, exorcisms and healings
The powers do their worst and kill him on the cross
In the resurrection God overturns their verdict and defeats death
The powers are disarmed and humanity is liberated
The Church lives in Christ's victory, awaiting the final destruction of death

positions.name: Satisfaction theory
positions.summary:
Anselm of Canterbury's satisfaction theory asks why God became human (Cur Deus Homo) and answers by reasoning about sin and justice. Every rational creature owes God the whole obedience of its will; to withhold it is to rob God of the honour due to him, not in the sense of wounding God's ego but of disordering the beauty and justice of creation. Such disorder cannot simply be overlooked. Justice requires either satisfaction (making amends beyond what was taken) or punishment. God, out of mercy, chooses satisfaction rather than the destruction of humanity.

But the debt is infinite and humanity already owes God everything, so no human can pay it, while only a human ought to pay it. Therefore only one who is both God and human can make satisfaction. Christ, being sinless, did not owe death; by freely giving his life he offered a gift of infinite worth that honours God beyond all that sin took away. Such a gift merits a reward, but the Son needs nothing, so the reward is given to those for whom he died, namely forgiveness for all who come to him. Aquinas later refined this into 'superabundant satisfaction' and combined it with merit, sacrifice and redemption, and Catholic teaching continues to use satisfaction language.

figures.name: Anselm of Canterbury
figures.bio: Born in Aosta, abbot of Bec in Normandy and later Archbishop of Canterbury. Known for 'faith seeking understanding' and the ontological argument, he wrote Cur Deus Homo as a dialogue with his pupil Boso, completing it in 1098 during exile in Italy.

works.author: Anselm of Canterbury
works.title: Cur Deus Homo (Why God Became Man)

figures.name: Thomas Aquinas
figures.bio: Aquinas argued that the incarnation and passion were not strictly necessary but most fitting, and that Christ's passion offered God a superabundant satisfaction through the greatness of his love and the dignity of his person. He combined satisfaction with merit, sacrifice, redemption and efficient causality.

works.author: Thomas Aquinas
works.title: Summa Theologiae

figures.name: Council of Trent
figures.profession: Ecumenical council of the Catholic Church
figures.bio: Trent's decree on justification teaches that Christ by his most holy passion merited justification for us and made satisfaction for us to God the Father, enshrining satisfaction language in Catholic doctrine.

works.author: Council of Trent
works.title: Decree on Justification

figures.name: David Bentley Hart
figures.bio: Hart argued that Anselm has been misread as a theorist of feudal honour and divine violence; properly read, Anselm presents God as freely restoring the gift of creation, in substantial continuity with patristic theology.

works.author: David Bentley Hart
works.title: A Gift Exceeding Every Debt: An Eastern Orthodox Appreciation of Anselm's Cur Deus Homo

figures.name: Richard Swinburne
figures.bio: Oxford philosopher who defends a satisfaction-type view in which reparation and penance are offered through Christ's life as a costly gift that sinners can use to make amends to God.

works.author: Richard Swinburne
works.title: Responsibility and Atonement

positions.context:
Anselm wrote against two backgrounds. First, he rejected the ransom view's suggestion that the devil had rights over humanity: the devil is a rebel creature and a thief with no just claim. Second, he answered Jewish and Muslim objections that incarnation and crucifixion were unworthy of God, aiming to show 'by necessary reasons' that the God-man was required. Critics since Harnack have read his concept of honour through the lens of feudal society, in which offences against a lord required compensation; defenders argue his 'honour' is the order of justice in creation.

Anselm's argument reshaped Western theology. Aquinas modified it, the Reformers recast it in terms of law and penalty (penal substitution), and Catholic teaching retains it (Trent; Catechism of the Catholic Church 615-616). Anselm explicitly contrasted satisfaction with punishment ('either satisfaction or punishment'), which is a key difference from penal substitution. Like other models it is usually combined with others: Catholic teaching speaks also of sacrifice, redemption, victory and participation.
claims: Sin is a failure to render God the honour (the obedient will) due to him, disordering creation.
God's justice and the beauty of creation do not allow sin to be simply overlooked.
Justice requires either satisfaction or punishment; God mercifully chooses satisfaction.
Only a human ought to make satisfaction; only God can; therefore a God-man is required.
Christ's freely offered death, not owed by a sinless man, is a gift of infinite worth.
The reward merited by Christ is given to sinners as forgiveness and grace.

scriptures.reading: All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God: sin is failure to give God his due glory.
If I am a father, where is my honour? God's honour is real and offended by sin.
Christ's obedience to death is followed by exaltation: obedience merits reward.
No one takes Christ's life; he lays it down freely, so his death is a gift, not a debt.
Christ offered himself without blemish to God through the eternal Spirit.
Christ gave himself up as a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.
A single offering perfects for all time those being sanctified.
The gift far exceeds the trespass: one man's obedience abounds for many.

arguments.text: Forgiving sin without any satisfaction would treat sinners and the righteous alike and leave creation's order unrestored, which would be unfitting for a just God.
The 'only humans ought, only God can' argument explains why the incarnation was required, not merely a fitting option.
The New Testament speaks of Christ's death as an offering to God (not to the devil), which matches satisfaction rather than ransom.
By distinguishing satisfaction from punishment, it avoids the problem of God punishing an innocent: the Father receives a gift of love, not a penalty.
It became the backbone of Western atonement theology and remains part of official Catholic teaching (Trent, Catechism).
It accounts for the abundance language of Romans 5: Christ's obedience more than outweighs Adam's sin.

critiques.text: It isolates the death of Christ from his whole life and resurrection; the resurrection plays little role in Cur Deus Homo.
Dismissing the devil entirely loses the biblical theme of bondage to an enemy; Scripture does speak of rescue from the power of darkness.
Aulén called it the 'Latin' type: humanity (in Christ) offers to God, making God the object rather than the subject of reconciliation.
Honour and compensation reflect medieval feudal culture; a loving Father does not need compensation before forgiving, as the prodigal son shows.
It does not take divine wrath and the penalty of the law seriously enough; Scripture says Christ bore our curse, not merely offered a gift.
It ties God to a strict necessity of satisfaction; God as Ruler can relax the law, so long as his government is upheld.
Any theory in which God requires a death to restore order sacralizes violence, which the Gospels unmask.
Juridical categories of debt and merit miss the deeper problem of corruption and death, which needs healing, not compensation.

responses.text: Anselm's narrow question (why the God-man?) did not require a full theology of the resurrection; Aquinas and later Catholic theology integrate satisfaction with Christ's whole life and exaltation.
Satisfaction does not deny bondage; it denies the devil's rights. Humanity is enslaved because of its debt to God, which once paid frees it from the devil's power.
God is the subject throughout: God the Son freely makes satisfaction, and the whole plan is the Father's mercy. Hart argues Anselm's God is giver, not creditor.
Honour in Anselm is the right order of creation toward God, not a lord's ego; and the prodigal still had to return. Satisfaction is God's own provision of that return.
Anselm's alternative of satisfaction instead of punishment is a strength: it shows God's justice without depicting the Father punishing the Son.
Anselm's 'necessity' is the fittingness of God acting according to his own goodness, not a constraint imposed on God from outside.
Satisfaction is a gift of obedient love, not a sacred killing; those who killed Jesus sinned, while Christ's self-offering in the midst of that violence is what pleases God.
Aquinas presents satisfaction alongside sacrifice and efficient causality: Christ's humanity as instrument of the divinity heals and sanctifies. Juridical and medicinal images need not compete.

strawMen.strawMan: Anselm's God is a touchy feudal lord whose ego was bruised.
strawMen.correction: Anselm says nothing can increase or decrease God's honour in itself; dishonour refers to the creature's disordered relation to God and the resulting disorder in creation.

strawMen.strawMan: Satisfaction theory is the same as penal substitution.
strawMen.correction: Anselm presents satisfaction as an alternative to punishment; penal substitution holds that Christ bore the punishment itself.

strawMen.strawMan: It makes salvation a cold transaction without love.
strawMen.correction: Anselm's whole argument is framed by God's mercy and the Son's free love; Aquinas locates the value of satisfaction chiefly in Christ's charity.

positive: Brought rigorous argument to the question of why the incarnation and cross were needed.
Ended reliance on speculative ransom-to-the-devil theories in Western theology.
Took the seriousness of sin and the order of justice with full weight.
Shaped Catholic spirituality of reparation and the Mass as offering.
negative: Its feudal vocabulary is easily misunderstood today.
Isolated the death of Christ from his life and resurrection in much Western preaching.
Its language of merit and satisfaction became entangled in late medieval penitential practices the Reformers attacked.
Can encourage a view of God as primarily concerned with debts.

adherents: Roman Catholic Church (Trent; Catechism 615-616), usually alongside other models
Thomist and Anselmian philosophical theologians
Many Anglicans and some Lutherans in modified forms
Analytic philosophers of religion defending reparative accounts
sequence: Humanity was created to render God the honour of an obedient will
Sin withholds that honour and disorders creation, incurring a debt
Justice requires either satisfaction or punishment
Only humanity owes the debt, yet only God can pay it
The God-man freely offers a death he did not owe, a gift of infinite worth
His offering merits a reward he does not need
The reward is given to sinners as forgiveness and restored grace

positions.name: Moral influence theory
positions.summary:
The moral influence (or moral exemplar) theory holds that the primary saving effect of Christ's life and death is on human hearts. Humanity's problem is not that God is unwilling to forgive, but that we are estranged, fearful and unloving toward God. In Christ, especially in his willingness to suffer and die for his enemies, God displays a love so great that it awakens answering love in us. This love frees us from the fear of punishment, moves us to repentance, and unites us to God, and by it we are justified and transformed.

Peter Abelard is regarded as its originator because of a famous passage in his commentary on Romans 3, though his own theology also uses language of Christ bearing our sins and interceding for us. The view became prominent in nineteenth- and twentieth-century liberal Protestantism (Schleiermacher in a qualified way, Horace Bushnell, Hastings Rashdall) and remains attractive to those who find objective models morally troubling. Almost all traditions include a moral-influence element; the debate is whether it is the whole of atonement or one effect of a deeper objective work.

figures.name: Peter Abelard
figures.bio: Brilliant and controversial Paris teacher, famous also for his relationship with Héloïse. In his Romans commentary he questioned the ransom theory and stressed that Christ's death reveals and kindles love. Bernard of Clairvaux attacked his teaching, and propositions attributed to him were condemned at the Council of Sens (1141).

works.author: Peter Abelard
works.title: Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans

figures.name: Horace Bushnell
figures.bio: Hartford pastor whose The Vicarious Sacrifice argued that Christ's sacrifice is 'vicarious' in the way all love bears others' burdens, and that its purpose is to restore humanity to God by the power of that love.

works.author: Horace Bushnell

positions.context:
Abelard taught in Paris in an age when Anselm had recently rejected the devil's rights. Abelard went further, asking why God would need any price, whether to the devil or to himself: how could the death of an innocent please God? His answer was that God, out of love, became human and persevered in teaching us by word and example unto death, binding us to himself by love. Bernard of Clairvaux denounced this as reducing Christ's work to example, and the Council of Sens (1141) condemned propositions drawn from Abelard's teaching.

The view revived in the Enlightenment and nineteenth century amid moral objections to penal theories (Socinians had already argued that God could forgive freely). Bushnell, Ritschl, Rashdall and others developed it. Twentieth-century critics such as P. T. Forsyth and James Denney argued that love shown by an act that achieves nothing is not intelligible. Contemporary scholars often note that Abelard himself combined this emphasis with other themes, and that subjective effects are affirmed in virtually every tradition alongside objective ones.
claims: God is always willing to forgive; the obstacle to reconciliation is on the human side.
Christ's life and death reveal the depth of God's love for sinners.
This revelation awakens repentance, love and trust in human hearts.
Love, not fear of punishment, is the true basis of obedience.
Justification is inseparable from the transforming love Christ kindles.
Christ's example calls believers to the same self-giving love.

scriptures.reading: God shows his love in that while we were still sinners Christ died for us.
God so loved the world that he gave his Son; love is the source and meaning of the cross.
In this is love, that God loved us and sent his Son; and (4:19) we love because he first loved us.
The love of Christ compels us, so that we no longer live for ourselves.
No greater love than to lay down one's life for friends.
Christ suffered for us, leaving an example that we should follow in his steps.
The father forgives the prodigal freely without demanding compensation.
When lifted up, Christ draws all people to himself: the cross draws by its attraction.

arguments.text: The New Testament repeatedly presents the cross as the demonstration of God's love, and love as what draws and transforms.
Jesus forgave sins freely during his ministry, before the cross, and taught a Father who forgives without payment.
Punishing an innocent person to permit forgiveness is morally incoherent; real forgiveness does not require payment.
Salvation must change the person; a theory that addresses only God's side or a legal status leaves the heart untouched.
Abelard was building on patristic themes of Christ as teacher and example (e.g. Augustine's emphasis on God's love in the incarnation).
Reconciliation in Paul is always of the world to God, never of God to the world, implying the change needed is in us.

critiques.text: Example alone cannot heal a fallen nature; humanity needs a new head, not only a moving spectacle.
Captives need release, not inspiration; a slave moved by the master's kindness is still a slave unless freed.
It ignores the objective powers of sin, death and evil that hold humanity and cannot be dispelled by changed feelings.
If nothing objective is accomplished, why was the death necessary? Bernard of Clairvaux charged that Abelard reduced the passion to an example.

A death is only a demonstration of love if it does something for us (James Denney's point that a man who drowns himself to show love to someone not in danger proves nothing); the love of the cross presupposes substitution.
It gives no account of how God upholds his moral law while forgiving; mere display of love risks implying that sin does not matter.
Girardians agree the cross reveals, but argue it reveals our violence as well as God's love; moral influence lacks an account of why humans kill.
It is too external: salvation is not only being moved by Christ but being united to him and sharing his divine life.

responses.text: The love revealed in Christ is not merely an example but the presence of God drawing people into communion; Schleiermacher and others speak of Christ communicating new life.
The 'slavery' is of the will and affections; love is precisely what frees the will from fear and sin.
The powers rule by fear, lies and distorted desire; the revelation of God's love undermines their grip at its source.
The death was necessary to show love to the uttermost in a world that kills the righteous; love that stopped short of death would be less than total.
Christ's death does achieve something: it reconciles us by changing us. Denney's analogy assumes the danger is from God; the danger is our estrangement, and Christ enters it to reach us.
The cross shows the seriousness of sin by revealing what sin does to Love incarnate; that is a stronger deterrent than a legal example.
Many moral-influence theologians welcome the point; revelation of human sin and of divine love belong together.
Love unites: Abelard spoke of being joined to God by love, which is a participatory idea; the theories differ more in vocabulary than substance here.

strawMen.strawMan: Moral influence says Jesus was just a good example and nothing more.
strawMen.correction: Proponents typically hold that God is personally present and active in Christ; the cross is God's own self-revealing love, not merely a human role model.

strawMen.strawMan: Abelard taught only a subjective theory.
strawMen.correction: Abelard's writings also speak of Christ bearing the penalty of our sins and interceding for us; the 'pure' subjective theory is more a modern development.

strawMen.strawMan: It denies that sin is serious.
strawMen.correction: Rashdall and Bushnell regarded sin as grave estrangement; they deny only that punishment must be transferred for forgiveness to be possible.

positive: Puts God's love at the centre of the atonement.
Insists that salvation must transform character and relationships.
Answers moral objections that other models can provoke.
Inspires imitation of Christ and costly service.
negative: Can reduce Christ to a teacher and example if separated from incarnation and resurrection.
Struggles to explain why the death in particular was required.
Can make salvation depend on the strength of human response.
Became associated with liberal theology's loss of other doctrines, making it suspect to many.

adherents: Many liberal and progressive Protestants
Unitarian and some Universalist traditions
Some process and liberation theologians in modified forms
Present as a secondary element in nearly all traditions

God, already willing to forgive, comes near in Christ
Christ lives and dies in self-giving love, even for his enemies

Love unites them to God and fulfils the law
Forgiven, they are transformed into Christ's likeness

positions.name: Penal substitution
positions.summary:
Penal substitution holds that on the cross Christ bore, in the place of sinners, the penalty that God's justice rightly requires for sin. God is holy and just; sin is not only a debt of honour but a violation of his law that deserves condemnation, death and wrath. Because God is also loving, he does not abandon sinners to that judgment, but neither does he set justice aside. Instead God himself, in the person of his Son, takes the penalty upon himself. Christ's death propitiates God's wrath and expiates sin, so that God is both 'just and the justifier' of those who have faith in Jesus (Rom 3:26). Through faith, believers are united to Christ: their sin is reckoned to him and his righteousness is reckoned (imputed) to them.

Defenders stress that this is not an angry Father punishing an unwilling third party: the Father, Son and Spirit act together in love; the Son freely gives himself; and the substitution is possible because Christ is both God and the representative head united with his people. John Stott called it the 'self-substitution of God'. Most proponents hold it alongside other models, often arguing that substitution is the foundation that makes victory, example and reconciliation possible.

positions.context:
Elements of penal substitution appear in patristic writers (e.g. Eusebius of Caesarea and others speak of Christ bearing our punishment), though defenders and critics dispute how central such statements are. The view was systematized in the Reformation, when Luther and Calvin recast Anselm's satisfaction in terms of law, penalty and the curse, linking it closely to justification by faith alone and imputed righteousness. Socinians attacked it in the late sixteenth century; Reformed scholastics such as Turretin defended it, and it became standard in Protestant confessions (e.g. the Westminster Confession speaks of Christ fully satisfying the justice of his Father).

In the twentieth century C. H. Dodd argued that hilastērion means expiation rather than propitiation, and Leon Morris answered him. Since the 1990s the view has been sharply criticized (e.g. Joel Green and Mark Baker; Steve Chalke's 2003 'cosmic child abuse' remark), and vigorously defended (Pierced for Our Transgressions, 2007). Most defenders today hold it as the central model among several and affirm Christus Victor and exemplary themes alongside it.
claims: God is holy and just; sin deserves his righteous judgment and death.
God's love does not set aside his justice but satisfies it.
Christ, the sinless Son, freely bore the penalty due to sinners in their place.
His death propitiated God's wrath and expiated sin.
Through faith, sin is imputed to Christ and his righteousness imputed to believers.
The triune God acts together in love: the Father gives, the Son gives himself, the Spirit applies.
Substitution is the foundation for Christ's victory over the powers and for new life.

scriptures.reading: The Day of Atonement scapegoat bears the people's iniquities, picturing transfer of guilt.
The Servant is pierced for our transgressions; the LORD lays our iniquity on him; he bears the sin of many.
God put Christ forward as a propitiation, to show he is just and the justifier.
God condemned sin in the flesh of his Son.
God made him to be sin for us so that we might become his righteousness.
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.
He bore our sins in his body on the tree.
Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous.
The cry of dereliction expresses Christ's experience of the judgment due to sin.
He is the propitiation (hilasmos) for our sins.

arguments.text: Isaiah 53, the Old Testament text most used by the New Testament to interpret Jesus' death, speaks repeatedly of the Servant bearing others' iniquities and punishment.
Paul's argument in Romans runs from the revelation of God's wrath (1:18) to propitiation (3:25) to 'no condemnation' (8:1): the problem of wrath is resolved at the cross.
The sacrificial system involves substitution (a life for a life) and the laying of hands to identify the offerer with the victim.
If God simply overlooked sin, he would not be just; a judge who acquits the guilty without satisfaction is unjust (Prov 17:15). Penal substitution shows how God remains just while justifying.
It provides assurance: if Christ has borne the full penalty, there is no condemnation left for the believer.
Statements that Christ bore our punishment appear in patristic writers before the Reformation, and the model has sustained the evangelical missionary movement for centuries.

critiques.text: It narrows salvation to a legal transaction at the cross, leaving Christ's life, resurrection and the renewal of human nature as secondary.
It makes the Father the one who must be paid, whereas patristic writers saw the ransom as rescue from the enemy, not payment to God.
Aulén argued it makes God the object rather than the subject of reconciliation and risks setting the Father against the Son.
Anselm insisted on 'satisfaction or punishment'; turning satisfaction into punishment makes the Father punish the innocent Son, which Catholic theology avoids.
Transferring punishment from the guilty to the innocent is morally incoherent; guilt is not transferable, and genuine forgiveness does not require payment.
If Christ paid the exact penalty, God is owed nothing and forgiveness is not grace; and if the payment is for all, all must be saved, or else payment was made for some only (limited atonement).
It sacralizes violence: God appears to need a victim to be appeased, the very logic of the scapegoat the Gospels expose.
Orthodox theologians object that it imports Western legal categories and implies a division in God's will, with wrath appeased by the Son's suffering.

responses.text: Penal substitution is not meant to be the whole of salvation; defenders affirm union with Christ, resurrection and new creation, but argue they rest on the removal of guilt.
Scripture presents Christ's death as an offering to God (Eph 5:2) and the ransom as from the curse of the law (Gal 3:13), not to the devil.
God is the subject: 'God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself' (2 Cor 5:19). The Father sends the Son in love; the Son gives himself; there is no division of will in the Trinity.
Christ is not an innocent third party but the head and representative of his people, united to them; what he bears, he bears as one with them and as God himself.
Human law permits sureties to pay debts, and the union between Christ and believers makes the substitution personal rather than arbitrary. Forgiveness is costly: the forgiver absorbs the cost.

Grace lies in God's providing the payment himself; Reformed theologians accept particular redemption, while others (e.g. Amyraldians, many evangelicals) hold that Christ's death is sufficient for all and applied through faith.
The cross is not humans offering a victim to appease God but God giving himself; the human violence is condemned, while God uses it to bear judgment on sin.
Wrath language is biblical (Rom 1:18; John 3:36), not merely Western; defenders also note patristic and liturgical texts that speak of Christ bearing our condemnation.

strawMen.strawMan: Penal substitution is 'cosmic child abuse': an angry Father beating a victimized Son.
strawMen.correction: Proponents insist the Son freely gives himself, the triune God acts with one will in love, and Christ is a grown adult and divine person, not a child acted upon.

strawMen.strawMan: It means God loves us only because Jesus changed his mind.
strawMen.correction: The cross flows from God's love (John 3:16; Rom 5:8); propitiation is God's own loving provision, not a bribe that changes God's attitude.

strawMen.strawMan: It is the only model evangelicals accept.
strawMen.correction: Major defenders (Stott, Packer) explicitly affirm victory, revelation and example; they argue only that substitution is central.

positive: Gives strong assurance of forgiveness and freedom from condemnation.
Takes sin, justice and divine holiness with full seriousness.
Has energized evangelical preaching, conversion and missions worldwide.
Integrates closely with justification by faith and grace.
negative: Popular presentations can portray God as angry and the Father as opposed to the Son.
Critics argue it can sanction violence or passive acceptance of suffering.
Can reduce salvation to a legal status with little emphasis on transformation.
Debates over the extent of atonement have divided Protestants.

Confessional Lutherans (with victory themes)
Most Baptist and evangelical churches
Many Anglicans (Thirty-Nine Articles, Article 31's language of 'satisfaction')
Global evangelical and Pentecostal movements

positions.name: Governmental theory
positions.summary:
The governmental theory, associated with the Dutch jurist and theologian Hugo Grotius, views God chiefly as the moral Ruler of the universe rather than as a private creditor or offended party. As Ruler, God may lawfully relax the penalty of his law for the sake of mercy, but he cannot simply ignore sin without weakening the authority of his moral government and encouraging further rebellion. Christ's death is therefore a public exhibition of God's hatred of sin and of what sin deserves. It is a genuine penal example, suffered by Christ on behalf of sinners, but it is not the exact equivalent of the punishment each sinner owed.

Because the law's authority has been vindicated before the universe, God can freely pardon those who repent and believe without compromising justice. Grotius presented the view as a defence of the 'catholic' doctrine of satisfaction against Socinus, but it became a distinct model. It was developed in New England theology (Jonathan Edwards Jr., Joseph Bellamy), in Charles Finney's revivalism, and in Methodist systematics (John Miley), where it fitted Arminian convictions that Christ died for all and that salvation is conditional on faith.

positions.context:
Faustus Socinus argued that satisfaction and forgiveness are incompatible: if a debt is paid, nothing is forgiven, and punishment of an innocent is unjust. Grotius, trained in law, responded by distinguishing God as an offended private party from God as a public Ruler. A ruler may relax a penal law for good reasons, provided he does so in a way that maintains the law's authority. Christ's suffering is that way.

Reformed theologians such as Turretin and later Charles Hodge criticized Grotius for weakening the necessity of satisfaction. In New England, the followers of Jonathan Edwards (the 'New Divinity') adopted governmental ideas, and Finney carried them into revivalism. Methodist theologians such as Miley made it a standard Wesleyan account, though other Wesleyans hold penal substitution. Today the view has fewer formal adherents but is defended by some Arminian and holiness writers. It is often combined with other models, especially moral influence and example.
claims: God relates to creatures as moral Governor, not merely as private creditor.
God's law expresses his good order for the universe and must be upheld.
God as Ruler can relax the penalty of the law, but not without vindicating it.
Christ's suffering is a penal example demonstrating sin's evil and God's justice.
Christ died for all; forgiveness is offered to all on condition of repentance and faith.
The atonement makes forgiveness consistent with the moral order and motivates holiness.

scriptures.reading: God displayed Christ to demonstrate his righteousness, because of his forbearance of past sins: the key governmental text.
The LORD was pleased for his righteousness' sake to magnify the law and make it honourable.
Righteousness and justice are the foundation of God's throne: God rules a moral kingdom.
Without shedding of blood there is no forgiveness, a principle of public order.
Christ gave himself a ransom for all, consistent with a universal provision.
Christ is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world.
God condemned sin in the flesh so that the law's righteous requirement might be fulfilled in us.
It pleased the LORD to bruise him; the Servant's suffering accomplishes God's righteous purpose.

arguments.text: Romans 3:25-26 says the cross demonstrates God's righteousness in view of his forbearance: a public display that vindicates his government.
It resolves Socinus's dilemma: forgiveness is genuine because God relaxes the strict penalty, while justice is maintained by the public display in Christ.
It fits unlimited atonement: Christ's death provides for all without implying that all are automatically saved, since pardon is conditional on faith.
Scripture presents God as King and Lawgiver whose concern is the welfare of his whole realm.
It drove the evangelistic urgency of Finney's revivals and nineteenth-century holiness movements by stressing human responsibility and the universality of grace.
It shows why the cross deters sin and motivates holiness: it reveals what sin deserves and how seriously God takes it.

critiques.text: Its focus on public order is external to the person of Christ; it says little about the renewal of human nature in him.
It loses the biblical emphasis on liberation from bondage to evil; salvation becomes a matter of legal policy.
It makes the cross a lesson to the universe rather than a decisive act that defeats the powers.
By making satisfaction optional (God may relax the law), it undermines the fittingness of the God-man's work and makes the cross a choice among possible means.
Punishing Christ not for our sins but as a public example is more unjust than penal substitution; and it leaves believers with no real removal of guilt, only a policy decision.
If the cross works by its effect on observers, it is effectively a moral-influence theory with legal vocabulary; why speak of penalty at all?
Making a public example of an innocent to deter others is precisely the logic of the scapegoat that the Gospels expose.
It reflects early modern ideas of the state and law more than the biblical and patristic picture of God as healer and giver of life.

responses.text: Governmental theorists affirm regeneration by the Spirit as the application of the atonement; the theory explains the basis of pardon, not the whole of salvation.
Liberation is affirmed: pardoned sinners are freed from condemnation and empowered for holiness; the theory addresses how liberation is just.
The exhibition is itself victory: sin's claim that God is indifferent or unjust is answered before all creation.
God freely chose the most fitting means; that the law could be relaxed does not make the cross arbitrary, since only it achieves both mercy and the honour of the law.

Christ suffers on behalf of sinners and because of their sins, and his suffering is penal in character; what is denied is a strict quantitative equivalence, not substitution. Guilt is removed by pardon.
The influence is not merely emotional but governmental: it secures the moral order objectively, so God can pardon justly.
Christ is no unwilling victim chosen by a crowd; he freely offers himself, and God's purpose is to save all, not to secure peace by excluding one.
Scripture itself uses the language of kingdom, throne, law and judge; Grotius drew on biblical images of divine kingship, not only modern politics.

strawMen.strawMan: The governmental theory says Christ did not suffer for our sins at all.
strawMen.correction: Grotius and Miley hold that Christ suffered for sinners and because of their sins; they deny only that his suffering was the exact equivalent of each sinner's penalty.

strawMen.strawMan: It is just a deterrence theory where God makes an example of an innocent man.
strawMen.correction: Christ is the willing, divine Son acting for the salvation of all; the 'example' vindicates God's law so that pardon can be offered.

strawMen.strawMan: It is a liberal theory that denies the need for atonement.
strawMen.correction: It arose to defend the necessity of Christ's satisfaction against Socinianism and was held by revivalists and holiness preachers.

Supports universal offer of the gospel and human responsibility.

Its reliance on legal theory can feel abstract to modern readers.
Associated with Finney's 'new measures', which critics blame for shallow revivalism.

positions.name: Mimetic (scapegoat) theory
positions.summary:
The mimetic or scapegoat theory draws on the work of the French literary theorist and anthropologist René Girard. Girard argued that human desire is 'mimetic': we learn what to want by imitating others, which leads to rivalry and spreading conflict. Archaic societies resolved such crises by uniting against a single victim, a scapegoat, whose expulsion or death brought sudden peace. Because that peace seemed miraculous, the victim was later remembered as guilty and sacred, and the episode was disguised in myth and repeated in ritual sacrifice. Culture, religion and law, on this account, rest on hidden founding violence.

The Bible, Girard argued, progressively tells such stories from the victim's point of view (Abel, Joseph, Job, the psalms of lament, the suffering Servant), and the Gospels complete this revelation. Jesus is the innocent victim against whom all unite (Herod and Pilate become friends, the crowd turns, the disciples flee), but the Gospels insist he is innocent, and his resurrection vindicates him. The cross thus exposes and disarms the scapegoat mechanism. Theologians such as S. Mark Heim, Raymund Schwager and James Alison developed this into an atonement theology: God does not require sacrifice; God enters the place of the victim to end sacrifice, and forms a new community that imitates Christ rather than rivals.

positions.context:
Girard's mimetic theory emerged from literary and anthropological work in the 1960s and 70s, not from theology. His conversion to Catholicism (around 1959) shaped his reading of the Gospels as a unique revelation. Early on he rejected 'sacrificial' readings of the cross entirely; later (from the 1990s) he acknowledged that Christ's self-giving could be called sacrifice in a different sense than archaic sacrifice.

Theologians from Catholic, Mennonite, Baptist and other traditions adopted his ideas, attracted by its account of violence and its critique of 'God requires blood' readings. Critics include anthropologists who doubt a single universal origin of culture, and theologians who argue it reduces sin to social mechanisms or leaves the cross without an objective Godward dimension. Like the other models, it is frequently combined with others, especially Christus Victor (as an account of the 'powers') and moral influence.

Archaic cultures achieve peace by uniting against a scapegoat, then sacralizing the victim in myth and ritual.
The Bible progressively exposes this mechanism by siding with the innocent victim.
Jesus willingly becomes the scapegoat, and the Gospels proclaim his innocence.
The resurrection vindicates the victim and reveals God's forgiveness rather than vengeance.
God does not need sacrifice; the cross ends the sacrificial logic.
The Spirit forms a community that imitates Christ and no longer needs victims.

scriptures.reading: Abel's blood cries out: the Bible sides with the murdered brother at the founding of civilization (Cain builds the first city, 4:17).
Caiaphas states the logic of the scapegoat: better that one man die than the whole nation perish.
Herod and Pilate become friends that day, the unifying effect of collective violence.
'They know not what they do': the persecutors are blind to the mechanism they enact.
Things hidden since the foundation of the world are revealed: Girard's title text.
Jesus names the blood of all the righteous from Abel onward, exposing a history of murder.
God desires mercy, not sacrifice, quoted by Jesus (Matt 9:13; 12:7).
Satan, the accuser who drives collective accusation, falls like lightning.
The crowd's verdict ('stricken by God') is overturned by the truth of the victim's innocence.
Peter tells the crowd they killed the Author of life in ignorance, yet God raised him.

arguments.text: The passion narratives emphasize the unanimity of the crowd, the reconciliation of enemies, and the innocence of Jesus, exactly the features of scapegoating made visible.
The prophets and Jesus criticize sacrifice in favour of mercy, suggesting God does not desire victims.
It explains why the cross is necessary without positing a God who demands violence: the cross is necessary to reveal and break the mechanism.
Girard's comparative study of myth found recurring patterns of crisis, collective murder and divinized victims, which biblical texts consistently invert.
It accounts for the social and political dimension of sin, the spread of rivalry and violence, as well as the personal.
Modern concern for victims, which Girard traced to biblical influence, shows the Gospel's revelatory effect working in history.

critiques.text: By centring a social mechanism, it underplays the incarnation and the renewal of human nature that Christ accomplishes.
It turns Satan into a name for a social process; the biblical devil is a personal adversary.
Many CV proponents welcome its account of the powers, but warn that it can collapse spiritual powers into anthropology.
It leaves no Godward dimension to the cross: Christ's offering to the Father, which Scripture affirms, becomes mere exposure.
Its saving effect is still revelation and imitation; it may be a sophisticated version of moral influence, with similar limitations.
It must explain away the many biblical texts in which God himself gives the Son, lays iniquity on the Servant, and acts in judgment; the cross is God's deliberate plan, not only human violence.
Its critique of sacrifice ignores that God commanded the sacrificial system in the Law; the Bible does not simply oppose sacrifice.
It describes how Christ breaks a cycle of violence, but not how humanity is healed of mortality and united to God.

responses.text: Only a fully human victim who is also the divine Son can reveal and break the mechanism from within; the theory presupposes the incarnation.
Girard used 'Satan' as the biblical name for the accusing, mimetic process; theologians in his school differ on whether there is also a personal being behind it.
Agreed that the powers are more than social; mimetic theory names one way they operate and need not exhaust them.
Heim and later Girard affirm Christ's self-offering to God in love; what they deny is that the Father needs a victim. The Godward dimension is obedience, not appeasement.
Unlike moral influence, it holds that something objective happens: the mechanism that structures human culture is broken and the victim is raised by God.
God's plan is to use human violence to undo it; texts of divine agency describe God's purpose through the evil (Gen 50:20), not God's desire for violence.
Old Testament sacrifice is read as a stage in revelation, regulating and progressively critiquing violence (substituting animals for humans, Gen 22) until the prophets call for mercy.
Alison and others link the end of rivalry with new creation: imitating Christ through the Spirit is a form of participation in divine life.

strawMen.strawMan: Girard says Jesus' death was just an unfortunate accident or a political murder.
strawMen.correction: Girardians hold that Jesus freely and deliberately went to the cross to expose the mechanism; it was necessary for revelation, not accidental.

strawMen.strawMan: Mimetic theory is purely secular sociology.
strawMen.correction: Girard regarded the Gospels as a divine revelation and the resurrection as real; theologians use the theory within Christian faith.

strawMen.strawMan: It denies any sin in individuals, blaming only 'the system'.
strawMen.correction: Each person participates in mimetic rivalry and in scapegoating; repentance is personal, as Peter's denial shows.

positive: Offers a strong theological critique of violence, scapegoating and persecution.
Links atonement to social ethics, reconciliation and nonviolence.
Provides fresh readings of passion narratives and Old Testament texts.
Engages secular disciplines (literature, anthropology) in conversation with theology.
negative: Its anthropological claims about the origin of culture are contested by many specialists.
Can minimize the Godward dimension of atonement and divine judgment.
Requires reinterpreting sacrificial texts in ways many find strained.
Its vocabulary is technical and can be hard for congregations to apply.

adherents: Girardian theologians in Catholic, Mennonite and mainline Protestant circles
Colloquium on Violence and Religion (academic network)
Some progressive evangelicals and peace-church theologians
Often combined with Christus Victor and moral influence

Rivalry spreads into a crisis of all against all

positions.name: Healing / participatory (theosis)
positions.summary:
The healing or participatory model, characteristic of Eastern Orthodox theology, understands salvation primarily as the healing of human nature and its union with God (theosis, or deification). The fundamental human problem is not chiefly a legal debt but a sickness: separation from God, the source of life, which brings corruption and death and enslaves the will to the passions. The eternal Word therefore takes a full human nature, body and soul, and in his own person unites it to divinity. 'What is not assumed is not healed', said Gregory of Nazianzus: Christ assumes everything human, including mortality, and heals it from within.

The cross is the point at which Christ enters death itself and destroys it, 'trampling down death by death', and the resurrection is the renewal of human nature with incorruption. Believers participate in this healed humanity through baptism, the Eucharist, prayer and ascetic struggle, by the Holy Spirit, growing by grace into what God is by nature, without ceasing to be creatures. Forgiveness, sacrifice and victory are all affirmed, but they are understood within this larger therapeutic and participatory vision.

positions.context:
The healing model grew from Irenaeus's recapitulation and was developed in the fourth-century debates over Christ's divinity and humanity. Athanasius argued that only one who was truly God could deify humanity, which is why the Arian view of a created Son could not save. The Cappadocians, Cyril of Alexandria and Maximus the Confessor deepened the theme, and later Byzantine theologians (Symeon the New Theologian, Gregory Palamas) linked theosis to prayer and the uncreated energies of God. The Orthodox Paschal hymn proclaiming that Christ tramples down death by death expresses its liturgical heart.

In the twentieth century Orthodox theologians in the West (Lossky, Florovsky, Meyendorff) presented this vision as an alternative to Western juridical models, sometimes polemically. Recent scholarship (e.g. Norman Russell) has traced deification in the Greek Fathers, and Western scholars have rediscovered participation in Aquinas, Calvin's union with Christ, and Luther (the Finnish school). Like the other models, it is held in combination: Orthodox liturgy also speaks of sacrifice, ransom and forgiveness.
claims: Humanity was created for communion with God and growth into his likeness.
Sin is separation from the source of life, leading to corruption, death and bondage to passions.
The Word assumed a complete human nature in order to heal it entirely.
Christ entered death and destroyed it from within; the resurrection renews human nature.
Salvation is participation in Christ's healed humanity by the Spirit, through the sacraments and ascetic life.
The goal is theosis: becoming by grace what God is by nature, without confusion of Creator and creature.

scriptures.reading: Believers become partakers of the divine nature, escaping corruption.
The Word became flesh: the incarnation is itself the beginning of healing.
He shared flesh and blood to destroy death and was made like his brothers in every respect.
By his stripes we are healed: salvation as healing.
That they may be one in us: participation in the communion of Father and Son.
We are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory by the Spirit.
Baptized into his death, we share in his resurrection life.
This corruptible must put on incorruption; death is swallowed up in victory.
Whoever eats Christ's flesh and drinks his blood abides in him and has life: Eucharistic participation.
'You are gods', cited by Jesus in John 10:34 and read by the Fathers as pointing to deification by grace.

arguments.text: Scripture describes salvation as union with Christ, sharing his life, being transformed into his image and partaking of the divine nature, not only as a legal verdict.
If the human problem is mortality and corruption, a legal acquittal alone would not solve it; what is needed is a change in human nature, which the incarnation provides.
The Nicene and Chalcedonian definitions were argued largely on soteriological grounds: only a fully divine and fully human Christ can heal and deify humanity.
The Gospels portray Jesus as healer; his healings anticipate the full healing of humanity in his death and resurrection.
It avoids setting God's justice against his love: God is not a party to be appeased but the physician who heals.
It is the continuous teaching of the Eastern churches and their liturgy, from the fourth century to the present.

critiques.text: Largely shared; the caution is that 'nature' language should not obscure Christ's personal, historical obedience, which Irenaeus stressed.
It can neglect the personal enemy whose dominion Christ broke; healing language alone may sound as if evil were merely an illness.
Healing is the fruit of victory; without the drama of conflict it risks becoming a gradual process rather than a decisive event.
It lacks an account of why the death of Christ in particular was needed, beyond entering mortality; the moral disorder of sin requires amends, not only healing.
Talk of transformed 'nature' can become impersonal and quasi-physical, bypassing the will and affections.
It downplays guilt, divine wrath and justification, treating sin as sickness rather than culpable rebellion; deification language risks blurring Creator and creature.
It says little about how God's law and moral order are upheld in forgiving sinners.
It can treat the crucifixion as an event between God and human nature in the abstract, ignoring the concrete human violence the passion narratives describe.

responses.text: Agreed: Maximus insists on Christ's real human will and obedience in Gethsemane; nature is healed through personal obedience.
The Orthodox liturgy is full of victory over the devil (e.g. the baptismal exorcisms); healing and liberation are two sides of one salvation.
The Paschal victory is decisive; participation is the ongoing appropriation of a victory already won.
Death is the consequence and power of sin; Christ must die to destroy death from within and to offer a perfect self-gift to the Father on behalf of all, as Athanasius says in On the Incarnation 9.
Theosis is deeply personal: it is the free cooperation (synergy) of the human will with grace, expressed in repentance, prayer and love.

Sin is both rebellion and sickness, and forgiveness is integral; but God's 'wrath' is understood as the experience of his love by those who reject it. Theosis is by grace and participation in God's energies, not essence, preserving the Creator-creature distinction.
God's 'law' is the life-giving order of communion; in healing human nature God restores that order more fully than a legal vindication could.
The Fathers' homilies on the passion attend closely to the betrayal and condemnation; Christ heals humanity precisely by bearing its violence without retaliation.

strawMen.strawMan: Theosis means humans become God in essence, a kind of pantheism.
strawMen.correction: The Fathers teach participation by grace in God's life and energies, not in his essence; the creature remains a creature.

strawMen.strawMan: Orthodox theology has no place for the cross or forgiveness.
strawMen.correction: The cross is central in Orthodox worship (e.g. the Exaltation of the Cross) and forgiveness of sins is proclaimed in every liturgy; the model frames them within healing.

strawMen.strawMan: The healing model is just 'salvation by incarnation' and makes the death optional.
strawMen.correction: Athanasius explicitly argues that the Word took a body so that he could die and destroy death; the death and resurrection are the core of the healing.

positive: Presents salvation as healing and life, appealing to those wounded by harsh images of God.
Holds incarnation, cross, resurrection, sacraments and spiritual life together.
Offers a high vision of human destiny and dignity.
Has enriched Western theology through renewed interest in union with Christ.
negative: Can seem vague about personal guilt and the forensic language of Paul.
Polemical contrasts between 'Eastern' and 'Western' models have sometimes caricatured both.
Its sacramental and ascetic framework can be hard to translate into non-liturgical traditions.
Deification language is easily misunderstood.

sequence: Humanity, made for communion with God, turns away and falls into corruption and death
The eternal Word takes a full human nature, body and soul
What he assumes he heals, uniting human nature to divinity
He enters death on the cross and destroys it from within
Rising, he renews human nature with incorruption
By the Spirit, baptism and the Eucharist, believers share his life
